opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most underappreciated parts of research. A lot of people assume that if you come up with a better idea, a better optimizer or a new attention variant or a new way of structuring computation, it'll naturally win. But in practice, the idea has to run fast on the hardware we actually have. If it doesn't, it doesn't matter how good it is on paper.

The way I think about it: every method has a theoretical benefit, say better convergence per step, better sample efficiency, or better quality at a fixed parameter count. But what you care about is quality per unit of wall-clock time, or per dollar. If your new method gives a 20% improvement per step but each step is 2x slower because there's no efficient kernel for it, you've lost. And people will rightly ignore it.

I saw this firsthand with second-order optimization. Preconditioning methods like Shampoo have been known for a while to give much better updates in some sense. But they involve operations like matrix roots and inverses that aren't what accelerators are built for. Accelerators love big dense matmuls in low precision. Ask them to do an eigendecomposition in high precision and you're fighting the hardware. So a huge amount of the work wasn't the math of the optimizer. It was figuring out how to restructure the computation, amortize the expensive parts, run them asynchronously, and pick numerics that hold up, so the method actually beats Adam on wall-clock time. That engineering is what turns an idea from a paper into something people use.

And there's a kind of lock-in effect. The hardware and software stack has co-evolved with the methods that are already popular. Transformers and Adam run extremely well because years of kernel work have gone into them. So any new method starts at a disadvantage. It's competing not just against the old idea but against all the optimization invested in it. That's what I mean by a bottleneck. It's a filter on which ideas survive, and it isn't purely a filter on quality.

So I'm excited about anything that lowers the cost of writing good kernels, whether better compilers, better languages for expressing these computations, or models themselves helping write and tune kernels. If a researcher can go from "here's my new update rule" to "here's a fast, fused implementation" in a day instead of three months, the space of ideas we can actually test at scale gets much bigger. I think a lot of good ideas are sitting out there right now because nobody has done the low-level work to make them fast.

r001.rationale: It says a method must improve quality per wall-clock time or dollar, and gives the example that a 20% per-step gain loses if each step takes twice as long.

r002.rationale: It points to operations such as matrix roots and inverses as poorly suited to accelerators and says popular methods have benefited from years of kernel work, leaving new methods at a disadvantage.

r003.rationale: It describes kernel writing and tuning as costly, but does not identify a shortage of people able to write low-level XLA code.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that a research idea only becomes real once it runs fast on the hardware you actually have. You can have a new attention variant, a new optimizer, a new sparsity scheme that looks great on paper, and in a small-scale experiment it might even show a nice loss curve. But the question that decides whether it matters is: at scale, does it hit the accelerator efficiently? And the honest answer is that most new methods don't, by default.

The reason is that the whole stack has been co-designed around a small number of operations. Dense matmul, standard attention, a handful of elementwise and reduction patterns. Those have had years of engineering poured into them, so they run close to the roofline. The moment you deviate, you fall off a cliff. Your new method might be two times fewer FLOPs in theory, but if the kernel is memory-bound, or if it breaks the fusion that the compiler was doing for you, or if it forces a layout change that costs a copy, you can easily end up slower in wall-clock time. And wall-clock is what we care about. Nobody trains on FLOPs.

So what happens in practice is the new idea gets evaluated against a highly optimized baseline with an unoptimized implementation of itself, and it loses, and people conclude the idea was bad. Sometimes it was. But often the comparison was just unfair. The second-order optimizer that needs a different reduction pattern, the attention variant that needs a custom tiling, the mixture-of-experts routing that needs a good scatter and gather. Each of those requires someone to sit down and write the kernel, think about the memory hierarchy, handle the sharding across chips. That is a scarce skill, and it is slow work. It can take weeks or months for one idea.

That gap is the bottleneck. The rate at which we can try ideas properly is limited not by how many ideas we have but by how many of them we can make fast enough to test honestly at scale. That is also why I find the compiler and kernel-generation side so interesting right now. If you can lower that cost, if the time from "here is a new op" to "here is a near-roofline kernel sharded across a pod" drops from weeks to hours, then the whole research loop speeds up. Many methods we dismissed might come back, and many we haven't thought of become cheap enough to explore.

r001.rationale: It says a method must run efficiently at scale and emphasizes wall-clock speed, but does not explain that its gains must justify additional compute cost.

r002.rationale: It explains that the stack is heavily optimized for a small set of standard operations and that novel methods can lose efficiency when they deviate from them.

r003.rationale: It identifies kernel-writing and optimization skill as scarce, but does not specify that the bottleneck is people able to write low-level XLA code.

astra-6.text:
Because a better method on paper doesn’t automatically translate into a faster model. You might reduce the amount of computation, but if your implementation moves more data around or launches lots of small operations, you can lose that advantage on the hardware.

And the baseline you’re competing with is usually very well optimized. So a new method can look worse initially simply because it hasn’t had the same investment in kernels. You need someone to understand the method, understand the hardware, and map one onto the other efficiently. That’s specialized work, and it slows down the loop between having an idea and knowing whether it delivers a practical improvement.

r001.rationale: The response says implementation overhead can erase a method’s advantage, but does not explain that its gains must justify its additional compute cost.

r002.rationale: It says a new method may initially look worse because it has not received the same investment in kernels as the optimized baseline.

r003.rationale: It describes kernel work as specialized, but does not identify scarcity of people able to write low-level XLA code.

sol-6.1.text:
Because a better method on paper doesn’t automatically translate into a faster computation on the hardware. You might reduce the number of operations, but if you introduce a lot of memory movement or break a large operation into many small ones, you can actually make things slower.

The methods we already use have highly optimized kernels behind them. A new method is competing with all of that engineering. So you can implement an idea, benchmark it, and conclude that it doesn’t help, when what you’ve really measured is the maturity of its implementation.

That makes the iteration loop expensive. To find out whether an idea is practically useful, you often need to do substantial kernel work first. Shortening that loop would let us explore more ideas and turn more of the promising ones into actual improvements.

r001.rationale: The response says fewer operations may still run slower because of memory movement or small operations, but it does not state that gains must justify additional compute cost.

r002.rationale: It contrasts mature kernels for existing methods with less mature implementations of new methods, but does not attribute the bottleneck to novel operations having received little optimization attention.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention a shortage of people able to write low-level XLA code.
